questions.question: Design a multi-tenant connector execution platform with bounded retries and per-tenant isolation.
questions.answer: I would clarify job sizes, latency targets, provider rate limits, tenant isolation and required delivery guarantees. A control API persists a job and publishes work through a durable handoff. Workers claim attempts, load tenant-scoped credentials and run connector strategies under bounded concurrency and rate budgets. Checkpoints allow large jobs to resume without restarting every record, while stable operation identifiers support safe retries. Results and progress are persisted independently from transient worker memory. I would expose queue age, provider errors and per-tenant throughput, with a dead-letter or manual-resolution path for permanent failures. The main trade-off is throughput versus strict per-key ordering and resource isolation; neither is free at high tenant counts.

followups.q: What happens when a worker dies?
followups.a: Its ownership must expire or be revoked safely, and a new attempt resumes from durable progress without accepting stale writes from the old attempt.

followups.q: What should not be in the queue payload?
followups.a: Long-lived plaintext credentials or giant datasets; carry identifiers and securely retrieve bounded task data.

questions.trap: Designing only a worker pool and leaving durable ownership, retries and tenant boundaries undefined.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD outline; key points and trade-offs included. No FS guide exists to link a full case study.

questions.question: Design a service that synchronizes enterprise users and groups into a SaaS tenant.
questions.answer: I would begin with the identity source of truth, supported SCIM operations, tenant boundaries and access-removal latency requirement. The service authenticates provisioning clients, validates schemas, maps stable external identities to internal users and applies changes with explicit uniqueness and concurrency rules. Group membership and deactivation need their own semantics, including what downstream entitlements must change. For async propagation I would commit durable change records and track delivery, reconciliation and retries rather than claim immediate global consistency. Audit records must support investigation without exposing unnecessary personal data. A periodic reconciliation job repairs drift. The key trade-off is fast provisioning response versus confirmed downstream completion, especially for security-sensitive access removal.

followups.q: What would you ask about deletion?
followups.a: Whether it means suspension, revocation, tombstoning or physical removal, and what legal or audit retention applies.

followups.q: How do you handle stale updates?
followups.a: Use supported version or precondition semantics and authoritative ordering rather than blindly apply an older change over a newer one.

questions.trap: Equating a successful provisioning response with completed revocation in every downstream system.
questions.notes: Unverified proposed HLD; not a fabricated description of Harsh's current service. Full guide unavailable.

questions.question: Outline a payment initiation API that handles retries and uncertain downstream outcomes safely.
questions.answer: I would define the payment state machine, idempotency scope and authoritative record before discussing scaling. A request uses a caller-scoped idempotency key bound to its meaningful payload. A durable record tracks accepted, pending, succeeded and failed or reconciliation-required states, with controlled transitions and auditability. A downstream timeout produces an uncertain outcome, not an automatic failure or permission to charge again. The service needs a provider reference and reconciliation mechanism, plus signed or authenticated callback handling with duplicate protection. Monetary amounts require exact representations and currency rules. Scaling can partition processing by a suitable ownership key, but correctness depends on atomic state transitions and recovery, not merely on putting requests into a queue.

followups.q: Can a repeated key with different payload be accepted?
followups.a: It should be rejected or handled under an explicit conflict contract, not silently reuse an unrelated result.

followups.q: Does HTTP timeout mean the customer was not charged?
followups.a: No. The provider may have acted; reconcile before creating another potentially duplicate operation.

questions.trap: Promising end-to-end exactly-once payment execution without defining recovery across the provider boundary.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD outline; no claim of payment-system work on the resume.

questions.question: Design a URL-shortening service with custom aliases, expiry and abuse controls.
questions.answer: Clarify redirect latency, creation volume, retention, custom-alias conflicts and abuse policy first. The write API validates destinations and atomically claims a unique short code; a mapping store serves redirects, with a cache for hot keys and expiry aligned to the record. A redirect service should distinguish permanent from temporary status because clients and browsers cache differently. The invariant is one active code maps to one destination until expiry; alias creation uses a uniqueness constraint, not a check-then-insert. If cache data is stale, invalidate on update or keep aliases immutable. Rate limits and malware checks reduce abuse. The trade-off is cache hit speed versus revocation freshness and storage cost.

followups.q: What happens when a custom alias is already taken?
followups.a: Reject it with a conflict; never overwrite another active mapping.

followups.q: Would you cache not-found results?
followups.a: Only briefly and with care, since newly created mappings could otherwise remain invisible.

questions.trap: Treating a cache as authoritative or ignoring browser caching and link-revocation requirements.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a notification platform that delivers email, SMS and push messages with user preferences and retries.
questions.answer: Clarify delivery volume, latency, priority, consent rules and whether the API promises accepted or delivered. A producer writes a durable notification intent, then channel workers partition work by tenant or recipient and call provider adapters under rate limits. The intent carries a stable ID for deduplication; attempts, provider receipts and terminal failures are recorded separately. Recheck consent and quiet hours at the agreed point, and route permanent errors to an operator-visible dead-letter path. Provider timeouts are uncertain, so retries need idempotency where available and duplicate-tolerant message semantics. Track queue age and delivery outcomes. The trade-off is fast acceptance with asynchronous delivery versus synchronous confirmation and provider coupling.

followups.q: Can the API guarantee delivery when it returns accepted?
followups.a: No; it guarantees durable acceptance, while delivery is a later observable state.

followups.q: How do you avoid a bad provider blocking all channels?
followups.a: Use per-channel bulkheads, bounded queues and independent retry policies.

questions.trap: Calling a queued notification delivered or retrying indefinitely without consent, deduplication and terminal handling.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a ride-dispatch system that matches nearby available drivers to a rider request and handles stale locations.
questions.answer: Clarify pickup radius, matching latency, location freshness, cancellation rules and expected geographic scale. Drivers send timestamped location and availability updates to a location service backed by a geo index; a dispatch service queries candidates, applies eligibility and sends a short-lived offer. A conditional assignment record ensures only one driver wins a ride, while offer expiry releases candidates. Stale location or dropped notifications trigger re-query rather than treating old coordinates as current. Partitioning by city improves locality but complicates cross-boundary trips and rebalancing. Monitor match time, stale-location rate and acceptance. The trade-off is nearest-driver quality versus response speed, battery/network load and regional capacity fairness.

followups.q: How do two dispatchers avoid assigning the same driver?
followups.a: Use an atomic compare-and-set or reservation with expiry and a single authoritative assignment state.

followups.q: What if a driver moves during matching?
followups.a: Use update timestamps and refresh candidates before final assignment when location age exceeds policy.

questions.trap: Choosing the closest coordinate without freshness, availability, assignment races or offer timeout semantics.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated. Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 7.16 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron)).

questions.question: Design inventory reservation for an online store where checkout may take several minutes and stock must not oversell.
questions.answer: Clarify whether stock is per warehouse, hold duration, backorder policy and acceptable availability staleness. An inventory service owns on-hand and reserved quantities; checkout atomically creates a time-bounded reservation only if available stock covers the request. A durable reservation ID links payment and order state. Confirmation converts reserved to sold, while cancellation or expiry releases capacity exactly once through a conditional transition. Expiry workers are recoverable and idempotent; the reserve operation itself checks expiry so delayed cleanup cannot oversell. For high-volume items, partition by SKU and warehouse. The trade-off is strongly consistent reservation writes versus higher throughput with temporarily stale catalog availability.

followups.q: Can the product page rely on cached stock?
followups.a: It can display an estimate, but checkout must claim stock against the authoritative inventory state.

followups.q: How do you handle payment success after reservation expiry?
followups.a: Define compensation or reacquisition behavior and make the order state visibly pending reconciliation.

questions.trap: Treating displayed availability as a guaranteed allocation or letting retries release the same stock twice.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design ticket booking for a popular event where many users compete for a limited number of seats.
questions.answer: Clarify reserved seating versus general admission, sale bursts, hold duration and payment timeout behavior. An inventory authority atomically moves seats from available to held with an owner and expiry; a booking workflow then confirms payment and turns the hold into a ticket. A uniqueness constraint on event-seat prevents double sale, and every command has an idempotency key. Queueing or virtual waiting rooms smooth a launch surge but must not imply a seat is guaranteed. Expiry and payment callbacks race, so state transitions compare expected state and reconcile uncertain outcomes. The trade-off is strict seat correctness and controlled throughput versus low-latency admission under extreme demand.

followups.q: Can a waiting-room token promise a seat?
followups.a: No; it controls admission order or rate, while inventory is confirmed only by an atomic hold.

followups.q: What if payment callback arrives after hold expiry?
followups.a: Reconcile payment and booking state, then confirm, refund or alert according to an explicit policy.

questions.trap: Using a queue as if it were inventory locking or letting delayed callbacks resurrect a sold seat.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a distributed rate limiter with per-client quotas, burst allowance and predictable behavior during datastore failure.
questions.answer: Clarify quota dimensions, window, burst, fairness and whether a rejected request should receive a retry hint. A gateway identifies a trusted client, then a shared atomic token-bucket or sliding-window operation checks and consumes quota; keys include tenant and route where policies differ. Local caches can reduce datastore calls but weaken global enforcement, so define the permitted overshoot. Set TTLs and bound key cardinality to control memory. If the limiter store fails, choose fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint risk and emit metrics. The trade-off is precise centralized enforcement versus availability, latency and state cost; do not claim exact global quotas from independent local counters.

followups.q: Why not use a local counter on every gateway?
followups.a: Traffic can multiply the effective quota across instances unless coordination or bounded overshoot is accepted.

followups.q: What should happen if the quota store is unavailable?
followups.a: Use an explicit endpoint risk policy, bounded fallback and alerting rather than one universal default.

questions.trap: Ignoring clock/window boundaries, datastore outages or the multiplication of quotas across replicas.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design webhook delivery for customer endpoints with retries, signing, ordering options and operational replay.
questions.answer: Clarify event volume, ordering scope, retention and customer retry expectations. The producer records an event durably, then delivery workers load the endpoint configuration, sign a canonical payload with a managed secret and send with a bounded timeout. Each attempt has an event ID, attempt number and response classification; exponential backoff and a terminal dead-letter state prevent endless retries. Endpoints are isolated by concurrency and circuit-breaker budgets, and manual replay preserves the original event identity. Delivery is at least once, so consumers must deduplicate. The trade-off is per-endpoint ordering and isolation versus queue throughput; SSRF controls and secret rotation are essential for customer-provided URLs.

followups.q: Can the sender guarantee exactly-once receiver effects?
followups.a: No; a timeout can occur after the receiver acts, so provide stable event IDs and require deduplication.

followups.q: How do you limit malicious endpoint URLs?
followups.a: Validate destinations, block private network ranges, recheck redirects and enforce egress controls.

questions.trap: Retrying webhooks without SSRF protection, receiver deduplication or a terminal failure path.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a large-file upload service that supports resumable transfer, integrity checks and safe publication after completion.
questions.answer: Clarify maximum size, allowed content, retention, access policy and whether clients upload directly to object storage. The API creates an upload session with owner, expected size and expiry, then issues scoped part-upload credentials. A manifest tracks received parts and checksums; completion verifies required parts and assembles or finalizes an immutable object version. Only after malware scanning and metadata validation should the file become visible. Expired sessions are cleaned asynchronously, while authorization and expiry are checked at completion. The trade-off is direct storage throughput and lower application bandwidth versus control-plane complexity, multipart cleanup and careful credential scope.

followups.q: Why not publish the object immediately after the last part?
followups.a: The manifest, checksum, malware scan and authorization checks may still fail.

followups.q: How do you resume safely?
followups.a: Persist part identifiers and checksums so retries can verify or replace only the intended part.

questions.trap: Trusting the filename or client MIME type and making an unscanned object publicly readable.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design an audit platform that captures security-sensitive changes from many services and supports reliable investigation queries.
questions.answer: Clarify event volume, query latency, retention, legal deletion and tamper-resistance needs. Services emit a versioned audit schema through a durable outbox or authenticated ingestion API; ingestion validates actor, tenant, action and timestamp, then appends to partitioned storage and indexes searchable fields. Preserve source event IDs for deduplication and never collect secrets or full payloads by default. Access to queries is separately authorized and itself audited. If indexing falls behind, durable raw events remain replayable and lag is visible. The trade-off is rich searchable indexing versus storage cost and privacy exposure; immutable retention must still match legal policy.

followups.q: Should search indexes be the source of truth?
followups.a: Usually retain an authoritative append-only event store so indexes can be rebuilt and audited.

followups.q: How do you handle late or duplicate events?
followups.a: Deduplicate by source event ID and retain event time separately from ingestion time.

questions.trap: Calling an ordinary mutable log table tamper-proof or indexing sensitive request bodies by default.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design autocomplete for a large product catalog with low-latency prefix suggestions and frequent updates.
questions.answer: Clarify languages, typo tolerance, freshness, ranking signals, query rate and privacy constraints. A catalog change stream feeds an index optimized for prefix lookup, while an API normalizes the query, applies tenant or locale scope and returns a small ranked result set. Cache popular prefixes with a short freshness bound and debounce at the client to reduce load. The index is derived, so updates carry versions and can be replayed after lag or corruption. Empty or stale suggestions must not expose unpublished products. The trade-off is richer ranking and fuzzy matching versus latency, index size and update complexity; measure query p95 and indexing lag.

followups.q: How do you avoid stale updates overwriting newer documents?
followups.a: Include source versions and apply only monotonic updates to the indexed record.

followups.q: Would you query the primary database on each keystroke?
followups.a: Usually no; a search-optimized index and bounded result set protect transactional storage.

questions.trap: Building suggestions from a cache without a freshness policy or indexing version guard.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a product catalog service that supports variants, localized attributes, filtering and frequent price or stock changes.
questions.answer: Clarify catalog size, attribute variability, localization, update rates and browse freshness. A catalog write API validates a product and stores canonical records; a change stream builds a search projection for filters and text lookup, while price and availability may come from more authoritative services. Product IDs and variant relationships remain stable, and unpublished items must not leak through stale indexes. Versioned updates and replay repair search lag. Use a cache for hot browse results with bounded staleness, not as inventory authority. The trade-off is flexible attributes and fast filtering versus schema governance, index cost and consistency between catalog, pricing and stock.

followups.q: Should stock be duplicated into the catalog?
followups.a: A browse hint may be copied, but final purchase availability belongs to the inventory authority.

followups.q: How do you handle schema variation by category?
followups.a: Use governed category schemas and validate attributes at write time rather than accept arbitrary untyped fields.

questions.trap: Treating a search index or cached stock count as the authoritative source for purchase decisions.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design one-to-one chat with message history, online delivery, offline recovery and per-conversation ordering.
questions.answer: Clarify message volume, retention, delivery receipts, multi-device behavior and acceptable online latency. Clients submit an idempotent message command to an authenticated conversation service, which verifies membership and appends a durable sequence-numbered message. A delivery gateway pushes to connected devices, while offline clients page history from storage using a cursor. Per-conversation ordering is maintained by partition ownership, not a global sequence. Reconnect resumes from the last acknowledged cursor, and duplicate sends deduplicate by client message ID. Presence is ephemeral and approximate. The trade-off is ordered per-chat writes versus hot-conversation throughput and storage; authorization must be checked on history reads and sends.

followups.q: Do you need one global message order?
followups.a: No; per-conversation order is usually the useful invariant and avoids global coordination.

followups.q: How does a client recover after disconnect?
followups.a: Resume from an acknowledged cursor and deduplicate messages by stable server or client ID.

questions.trap: Relying on WebSocket delivery as durable storage or promising global ordering across every conversation.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design collaborative text editing with concurrent edits, offline clients and conflict recovery.
questions.answer: Clarify document size, concurrent editors, offline duration, history retention and permission changes. Clients send operations against a known revision; a collaboration service orders or transforms them using a chosen CRDT or operational-transformation model, then persists a revision log and broadcasts accepted updates. The invariant is that replicas converge to one valid document state despite duplicates and reordering. Snapshots bound replay cost, while clients resync from a checkpoint after gaps. Permission checks apply to every operation, not just connection setup. The trade-off is algorithmic complexity and metadata growth versus low-latency concurrent editing; select a proven merge model and test partitions, reconnects and simultaneous edits.

followups.q: Can last-write-wins safely merge arbitrary text edits?
followups.a: Usually not; overlapping edits need a defined operation-transform or conflict-free data model.

followups.q: How do you bound reconnect replay?
followups.a: Create versioned snapshots and resume from the newest compatible checkpoint.

questions.trap: Broadcasting edits without a convergence rule, durable revision, or authorization on each operation.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a metrics platform that ingests high-cardinality service telemetry and supports dashboards and alerts.
questions.answer: Clarify sample rate, retention tiers, query windows, alert latency and cardinality limits. Agents batch and authenticate samples into regional ingestion endpoints, which validate timestamps and labels before writing partitioned time-series storage. Aggregation and downsampling reduce long-retention cost; query workers enforce time and series limits so one dashboard cannot exhaust the cluster. Alerts evaluate separately from interactive dashboards and preserve rule version and evaluation results. Backpressure or regional outage should buffer only within a bounded disk budget and expose dropped-sample counts. The trade-off is label richness and query flexibility versus cardinality cost and ingestion stability. Never accept unbounded user labels as free dimensions.

followups.q: Why can a unique user ID label be dangerous?
followups.a: It creates near one time series per user, multiplying index and memory cost.

followups.q: What if ingestion is overloaded?
followups.a: Apply backpressure, sampling or bounded dropping with explicit loss telemetry rather than unbounded queues.

questions.trap: Designing unlimited label cardinality or treating dashboard query load as free of ingestion impact.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a centralized log pipeline that supports search while preventing sensitive-data leaks and runaway ingestion cost.
questions.answer: Clarify ingestion volume, search freshness, retention, tenant isolation and regulated fields. Agents add service and trace metadata, redact known secrets locally, then batch logs into a durable regional buffer. Ingestion validates schema and applies further redaction before indexing; raw archives and searchable hot data can have different retention. Queries are tenant-scoped, rate-limited and audited. Backpressure uses bounded local buffers with visible drop counters, and index lag can be replayed from durable segments. The trade-off is searchable detail versus storage, privacy and cardinality cost. Redaction must happen before broad access, and the pipeline should never rely solely on application developers remembering every sensitive field.

followups.q: Should raw logs be kept forever for debugging?
followups.a: No; retention should reflect operational value, privacy constraints and storage cost.

followups.q: How do you correlate logs across services?
followups.a: Carry stable trace and request identifiers, while avoiding personal or secret values as correlation keys.

questions.trap: Indexing unredacted payloads broadly or creating an unbounded local buffer during an outage.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a feature-flag service that serves low-latency evaluations while supporting audited updates and emergency kill switches.
questions.answer: Clarify evaluation latency, client connectivity, targeting rules and how quickly an emergency disable must propagate. A control plane authenticates and validates versioned flag changes, records approver and audit history, then publishes snapshots to regional distribution. SDKs evaluate locally from an immutable snapshot for low latency and use a deterministic subject hash for rollout. Snapshot versions move monotonically; clients expose age and fall back according to flag risk when disconnected. Kill switches may use a faster invalidation channel but still need bounded propagation guarantees. The trade-off is local availability versus update freshness and rule complexity. Flags must not replace authorization checks.

followups.q: What if a client cannot reach the flag service?
followups.a: Use its last-known valid snapshot and per-flag fallback policy, while reporting staleness.

followups.q: Can a rollout hash use request ID?
followups.a: Use a stable subject key so the same user remains consistently assigned.

questions.trap: Making every request synchronously call the control plane or treating a flag as an access-control boundary.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design centralized configuration delivery with validation, staged rollout, rollback and secrets kept out of ordinary configuration.
questions.answer: Clarify consistency needs, rollout scope, client refresh behavior and whether applications can tolerate stale values. A control plane stores versioned, typed configuration with schema validation and approval; clients fetch signed snapshots and atomically swap only after local validation. Rollouts target cohorts and record acknowledgments, while rollback points to a prior immutable version. Secret references resolve through a separate secret manager with narrower access and rotation. If distribution is unavailable, clients use last-known-good configuration and expose its age. The trade-off is rapid centralized change versus blast radius and stale consumers; high-risk changes need staged rollout, health gates and a clear emergency path.

followups.q: Should clients observe partially updated settings?
followups.a: No; validate a complete snapshot and publish it atomically.

followups.q: How do you roll back a bad update?
followups.a: Promote a prior immutable version through the same auditable distribution path.

questions.trap: Mixing credentials into ordinary config files or applying unvalidated updates field by field.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a service for distributing and rotating credentials used by many backend services without downtime.
questions.answer: Clarify secret types, rotation deadline, service identity and whether providers allow overlapping credentials. A secrets control plane encrypts versions with managed keys, authorizes workloads by identity and audits reads; clients cache only for a bounded lease and never log values. Rotation creates a new version, distributes it, verifies consumers or health checks, then revokes the old credential after a grace period. Failed rollout pauses revocation and alerts operators. Access outage uses last-known credentials only within policy, with explicit expiry. The trade-off is availability through caching versus revocation speed. Rotation workflows must be idempotent and recover from interruption at each phase.

followups.q: Should the old secret be revoked immediately?
followups.a: Only after consumers have adopted the new version or policy explicitly accepts downtime risk.

followups.q: Can a service cache secrets indefinitely?
followups.a: No; bound cache lifetime to the required revocation and rotation response window.

questions.trap: Rotating a credential at the source but leaving consumers on stale cached values with no recovery path.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design an image upload and transformation pipeline that generates thumbnails and multiple formats reliably.
questions.answer: Clarify upload sizes, supported formats, privacy, transformation latency and retention. An upload API stores an immutable source object in quarantine and records metadata, then emits a durable processing job keyed by source version. Workers validate actual file content, scan it and generate deterministic derivatives to versioned object keys; a manifest marks the asset ready only when required outputs exist. Retries overwrite only the same derivative version and poison files go to an inspectable failure state. CDN delivery exposes only approved derivatives. The trade-off is asynchronous throughput versus time-to-preview and storage duplication. Bound decompression size and worker concurrency to protect against malformed images.

followups.q: Why use immutable source versions?
followups.a: A job can identify exactly which bytes it processed, even if the user later replaces the image.

followups.q: What if one thumbnail transform fails?
followups.a: Track per-derivative state and retry that output without reprocessing successful versions unnecessarily.

questions.trap: Trusting file extensions or publishing partially processed content before scans and required outputs finish.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a batch ETL platform that processes large source files with checkpoints, schema changes and recoverable failures.
questions.answer: Clarify file sizes, delivery cadence, correctness window, schema evolution and whether partial output is visible. An orchestrator records job and source version, then workers read bounded partitions, validate against a versioned schema, transform and write idempotent output chunks. Checkpoints advance only after output commit, using stable partition keys so a restart replays safely. Quarantine malformed rows with counts and secure samples; fail the job when error thresholds are exceeded. A manifest declares completion only when all partitions succeed. The trade-off is throughput through parallel partitions versus global ordering and cross-partition consistency. Monitor lag, retries and rejected records, and make reprocessing an explicit versioned operation.

followups.q: When should a checkpoint advance?
followups.a: After the corresponding output is durably committed, otherwise a crash can lose data.

followups.q: How do you roll out a changed transformation?
followups.a: Version it and define whether to replay into a new output set or perform a controlled migration.

questions.trap: Advancing source offsets before writes commit or claiming a multi-part job complete after only some partitions finish.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a double-entry ledger service that records transfers, supports balance queries and survives duplicate commands.
questions.answer: Clarify currencies, posting volume, correction policy, balance latency and audit requirements. A ledger API accepts an idempotent command, validates accounts and currency, then atomically appends balanced debit and credit entries under one transaction. Entries are immutable; corrections use reversing entries rather than edits. A balance projection accelerates reads but is rebuildable from the ledger and reports its freshness. Unique command IDs prevent duplicate posting, and account ordering or serializable constraints handle concurrent transfers. Replicas can serve lag-tolerant queries, but authoritative writes stay in one consistency boundary. The trade-off is strong posting correctness versus high write throughput and flexible cross-region availability.

followups.q: Should a correction update the old entry?
followups.a: No; append a compensating or reversing entry so history remains explainable.

followups.q: Can a read projection be the source of truth?
followups.a: It should be rebuildable from authoritative entries and expose its lag.

questions.trap: Updating a balance without matching ledger entries or silently editing posted financial history.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design order processing across inventory, payment and shipping services when no shared database transaction exists.
questions.answer: Clarify checkout response semantics, reservation expiry and acceptable recovery time. An order service persists an order state and outbox event, then coordinates inventory reservation, payment authorization and shipment through idempotent commands. Each participant reports a durable outcome; the order advances only through expected-state transitions. A timeout becomes unknown until queried or reconciled, not an automatic failure. If a later step fails, issue explicit compensations such as release inventory or void authorization and track compensation failure. A workflow log supports recovery after coordinator restart. The trade-off is eventual consistency and operational state complexity versus service autonomy and independent scaling.

followups.q: Is a saga a database rollback?
followups.a: No; compensation is a new business action and may fail, so its progress must be durable.

followups.q: What should happen after a payment timeout?
followups.a: Query or reconcile provider state before retrying a potentially duplicate authorization.

questions.trap: Claiming cross-service atomicity or treating a timeout as proof that a participant did nothing.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design recurring subscription billing with plan changes, failed payment recovery, invoices and duplicate-safe charge attempts.
questions.answer: Clarify billing calendars, proration, grace periods, currencies and provider callback behavior. A subscription record stores plan version, billing anchor and lifecycle; a scheduler creates one durable invoice occurrence per subscription and period with a unique key. Charge workers submit idempotent provider requests and record uncertain outcomes for reconciliation. Paid invoices transition subscription entitlement; failures enter a bounded retry and dunning policy before suspension. Plan changes create explicit effective-dated events so proration is reproducible. The trade-off is immediate entitlement updates versus provider confirmation and accounting accuracy. The system needs audit history, timezone-safe period calculation and a replay path that cannot charge the same period twice.

followups.q: How do you avoid duplicate monthly invoices?
followups.a: Enforce a unique subscription-and-period key when creating the durable billing occurrence.

followups.q: What does a provider timeout mean?
followups.a: The charge outcome is unknown; reconcile by provider reference or idempotency key before another attempt.

questions.trap: Using a timer without durable period identity or retrying uncertain charges as if they certainly failed.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a low-latency fraud-screening service that combines rules and risk signals without blocking every payment on a slow dependency.
questions.answer: Clarify decision deadline, false-positive tolerance, data residency and whether outcomes are approve, reject or step-up. The payment path sends a minimal authenticated request to a risk orchestrator, which evaluates versioned rules and bounded-time feature lookups; slow noncritical signals must not hold threads indefinitely. A decision record stores rule/model version, reason codes and feature freshness for audit. Timeouts follow an explicit policy such as safe decline or limited fallback based on transaction risk. Asynchronous feedback updates models but cannot retroactively change an already authorized payment. The trade-off is richer signal accuracy versus latency, availability and explainability; isolate dependencies and monitor decision drift.

followups.q: Should all dependency timeouts approve the transaction?
followups.a: No; fail-open or fail-closed depends on transaction risk and must be an explicit policy.

followups.q: How can a decision be reproduced later?
followups.a: Persist the decision version, reason codes and appropriately minimized input snapshot or references.

questions.trap: Letting an optional risk feature call block indefinitely or recording a score with no version or explanation context.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design an API gateway for authentication, routing, quotas and observability across independently deployed backend services.
questions.answer: Clarify protocol support, identity propagation, latency budget, tenant quotas and gateway availability goals. Stateless gateway instances validate tokens or delegate introspection, apply route policy and bounded rate limits, then forward to service discovery targets with deadlines and correlation IDs. Authorization remains enforced by services for domain ownership; gateway checks are defense in depth. Configuration is versioned and rolled out safely, and unhealthy instances are removed without dropping all traffic. Do not buffer unbounded request bodies or retry non-idempotent operations blindly. The trade-off is centralized cross-cutting consistency versus a critical path and policy concentration; keep business logic out and provide a controlled bypass strategy for internal health checks.

followups.q: Can the gateway be the only authorization layer?
followups.a: No; services must protect their own resources against alternate access paths and confused identity context.

followups.q: Should it retry every upstream timeout?
followups.a: No. Retry only when method semantics and idempotency make repetition safe within the deadline.

questions.trap: Turning the gateway into a monolithic business-policy service or assuming gateway authentication proves resource authorization.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design session storage across two regions with fast reads, failover and explicit logout behavior.
questions.answer: Clarify session lifetime, logout revocation target, regional outage model and whether users can tolerate reauthentication. Store opaque session identifiers with bounded expiry and minimal data; replicate by a defined consistency model, while sensitive authorization state remains verifiable by services. A logout or credential compromise needs a revocation mechanism whose propagation delay is measured, such as a versioned user epoch or regional revocation stream. During partition, decide whether to accept last-known sessions or fail closed for high-risk actions. The trade-off is global availability and local latency versus immediate revocation consistency. Avoid storing long-lived bearer secrets in logs or relying on sticky load balancing as durable session storage.

followups.q: Does sticky routing solve session durability?
followups.a: No; it only routes traffic and fails when the region or instance becomes unavailable.

followups.q: How do you limit stale sessions after logout?
followups.a: Use bounded token/session lifetime plus a revocation signal or authoritative epoch check for sensitive operations.

questions.trap: Claiming instant global logout while asynchronously replicating revocation without defining the allowed delay.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design metadata management for objects stored in blob storage, including ownership, versions, access and deletion.
questions.answer: Clarify object count, metadata query patterns, version retention, legal deletion and direct-upload requirements. A metadata API stores tenant, owner, object key, checksum, size, content status and version in a transactional database; blob storage holds bytes under opaque keys. Upload sessions bind scoped credentials to an expected object, and completion verifies checksum before marking metadata available. Reads authorize against metadata before issuing short-lived download access. Deletion uses a tombstone and durable cleanup workflow so database and blob removal can recover independently. The trade-off is fast metadata lookup versus duplicated state between SQL and object storage; reconcile orphan blobs and stale rows periodically.

followups.q: Which store is authoritative for ownership?
followups.a: The metadata service, with authorization checked before granting access to the blob.

followups.q: What if blob deletion succeeds but metadata update fails?
followups.a: Use a durable deletion state and reconciliation so retries converge without exposing the object again.

questions.trap: Assuming a database transaction can atomically commit with object storage or exposing predictable raw storage keys.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design an email campaign system that schedules large sends, honors unsubscribe state and limits provider load.
questions.answer: Clarify audience size, scheduling precision, unsubscribe latency, personalization and provider quotas. Campaign creation snapshots an approved audience definition and template version, then expands recipients into durable batches with idempotent send IDs. Workers apply per-provider rate limits and recheck suppression or consent immediately before delivery. Bounces and complaints feed a suppression store; retries distinguish transient provider failures from permanent addresses. Pause and cancel commands stop unsent batches but cannot retract delivered mail. The trade-off is campaign snapshot reproducibility versus honoring preference changes at send time. Monitor queue age, send rate and complaint rates, and provide a preview and bounded test send before bulk release.

followups.q: Does cancellation retract already sent email?
followups.a: No; it prevents future unsent work and must expose that delivery is already irreversible.

followups.q: When should unsubscribe be checked?
followups.a: At send time as well as audience creation, to honor changes made after scheduling.

questions.trap: Expanding an unbounded audience synchronously or retrying permanent bounces as temporary errors.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design appointment scheduling for providers in multiple time zones with conflict prevention, cancellations and reminders.
questions.answer: Clarify provider availability rules, slot duration, time-zone display, hold policy and cancellation limits. A scheduling service stores provider calendars with a named zone and materializes candidate slots; booking atomically claims a provider interval and records the client-facing zone for display. A unique or exclusion constraint prevents overlapping confirmed appointments. Temporary holds expire, but booking verifies time and availability in the transaction. Changes create versioned events for reminders, which workers deduplicate and cancel when appointments move. The trade-off is precomputed slots for fast browsing versus complexity around daylight-saving and calendar changes. Keep UTC instants authoritative while preserving recurring local-time rules.

followups.q: Why store a zone as well as UTC?
followups.a: UTC identifies an instant; a named zone preserves recurring local schedule rules and daylight behavior.

followups.q: How do you avoid duplicate reminders after rescheduling?
followups.a: Key reminders by appointment version and cancel or supersede older scheduled work.

questions.trap: Representing recurring local availability as fixed UTC offsets or relying on a read-before-book check.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design IoT telemetry ingestion for intermittent devices, duplicate messages, late data and device identity rotation.
questions.answer: Clarify device count, message size, offline buffering, freshness and retention. Devices authenticate with provisioned identities and publish sequence-numbered batches to regional gateways; ingestion validates device ownership and schema before durable buffering. A stream partitions by device or asset, deduplicates message IDs, and routes late samples to time-aware storage rather than discarding them blindly. Device credentials rotate through an enrollment lifecycle, and revoked devices are rejected at the edge. Backpressure must be bounded for unreliable links, with acknowledgments only after durable acceptance. The trade-off is low-latency streaming versus network cost, duplicate handling and late-arrival complexity. Track per-device lag and malformed payload rates without trusting device clocks as authoritative.

followups.q: Can device timestamps determine event order?
followups.a: Use sequence numbers and ingestion metadata too; device clocks can drift or reset.

followups.q: When should the gateway acknowledge a batch?
followups.a: After durable acceptance at the promised boundary, not merely after receiving bytes in memory.

questions.trap: Assuming reliable connectivity, unique delivery or trustworthy device time without explicit protocol support.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design change-data capture from a transactional database to downstream search and analytics consumers with replay and schema evolution.
questions.answer: Clarify source database load, end-to-end lag, ordering scope, retention and whether consumers need deletes. A CDC connector reads the database log from a durable offset and publishes versioned change envelopes keyed by entity ID. Consumers maintain their own offsets and apply events idempotently, using source sequence or version to reject stale updates. Initial snapshot and live-log handoff need a consistent boundary so rows are neither lost nor duplicated invisibly. Schema registry compatibility and tombstone semantics govern evolution. If a consumer fails, replay from retained offsets; monitor lag and log retention headroom. The trade-off is low-latency replication versus coupling to database internals and operational offset management.

followups.q: Can the same change be delivered more than once?
followups.a: Yes; consumers should checkpoint and apply idempotently using stable keys and versions.

followups.q: What if a consumer falls behind log retention?
followups.a: Rebuild from a fresh snapshot or archive, then resume at a coordinated log boundary.

questions.trap: Assuming a snapshot and live stream can be joined without a boundary or that CDC creates exactly-once consumer effects.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design an asynchronous export service for large tenant datasets with consistent snapshots, cancellation and secure downloads.
questions.answer: Clarify dataset size, snapshot consistency, retention, export formats and who may download results. The API authorizes and persists an export request with tenant, filters and schema version, then a worker reads a consistent snapshot or documented watermark and streams bounded chunks into encrypted object storage. A manifest records counts, checksum and completion state; only a completed export receives a short-lived download link. Cancellation stops future chunks and cleans partial output. Retries resume by stable partition or restart into a new object version. The trade-off is snapshot isolation and database load versus export freshness and completion time; throttle jobs and expire artifacts under explicit retention policy.

followups.q: Can a long export hold one database transaction open?
followups.a: That may retain snapshots and pressure storage; prefer a supported snapshot or watermark strategy with bounded duration.

followups.q: When is a download URL safe to issue?
followups.a: After completion and authorization, with short expiry and object scope limited to that export.

questions.trap: Building a large file in application memory or exposing a partial export through a reusable public URL.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a shared cache for frequently read tenant data with invalidation, hot-key protection and graceful datastore failure.
questions.answer: Clarify read/write ratio, freshness tolerance, value size, tenant isolation and availability expectations. Cache-aside clients use versioned tenant-scoped keys, bounded TTLs and size limits; authoritative writes publish invalidation or version changes after commit. A single-flight mechanism or request coalescing protects hot keys from stampedes, while jitter spreads expiry. On cache outage, only safe reads fall back to the source, with concurrency limits to avoid overwhelming it. Never rely on cached authorization as the sole access decision. The trade-off is reduced database load and latency versus stale data, invalidation complexity and an additional failure mode; measure hit rate, evictions and fallback pressure.

followups.q: Can TTL alone guarantee fresh data?
followups.a: No; it bounds staleness only if the maximum TTL is respected and clocks/refresh behavior are defined.

followups.q: What if the cache fails and every request falls back?
followups.a: Apply bulkheads, concurrency caps and controlled degradation to protect the source datastore.

questions.trap: Treating cache availability or cached permissions as correctness guarantees, or allowing unbounded fallback load.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a lease service for exclusive job ownership that remains safe when a paused worker resumes after lease expiry.
questions.answer: Clarify lease duration, clock assumptions, ownership scope and what resource the worker mutates. The coordinator grants a lease with a monotonically increasing fencing token and expiry using an atomic compare-and-set operation. Every write to the protected resource carries that token, and the resource rejects tokens older than the latest accepted value. Renewal is bounded and tied to owner identity; if renewal fails, the worker stops work. Expired ownership can be reclaimed, but the fencing check protects against a paused former owner. The trade-off is coordination availability and renewal traffic versus safe exclusivity. A lease without fencing cannot prevent stale writes after a long pause or network partition.

followups.q: Does lease expiry terminate the old process?
followups.a: No; it may keep running, so the resource must reject stale fencing tokens.

followups.q: Can workers use local clocks to decide ownership?
followups.a: No; rely on the coordinator's atomic state and treat local time only as a conservative stop signal.

questions.trap: Assuming lease timeout physically stops the former owner from writing to the protected resource.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design a personalized activity feed that balances freshness, celebrity fanout and stable pagination.
questions.answer: Clarify feed freshness, follow graph size, ranking complexity and pagination guarantees. For ordinary authors, publish events into per-recipient inboxes asynchronously; for high-fanout accounts, store posts once and merge them at read time to avoid enormous write amplification. A feed service filters privacy and blocks at read time, ranks a bounded candidate set and uses a stable cursor based on score plus unique post ID. Event IDs deduplicate fanout jobs, and graph or feed lag is observable. The trade-off is write cost and freshness versus read latency and ranking flexibility. Deletions and privacy changes require invalidation or read-time enforcement so stale feed copies do not leak content.

followups.q: Why use a hybrid fanout model?
followups.a: It limits write explosion for very large audiences while keeping common authors fast to read.

followups.q: Can the feed cache override a privacy change?
followups.a: No; enforce current access policy or invalidate affected copies before serving sensitive content.

questions.trap: Using offset pagination over a changing ranked list or copying private posts without a revocation path.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design full-text search across tenant documents with indexing lag, deletion propagation and strict access isolation.
questions.answer: Clarify document volume, query latency, permission complexity, freshness and deletion obligations. Source services emit versioned index events through durable delivery; indexers extract permitted fields, attach tenant and ACL metadata, and apply only monotonic versions. Search queries derive tenant identity from authenticated context and filter ACLs before returning snippets, with authorization rechecked for high-risk results. Deletes create tombstones and are monitored through index completion, not treated as done when merely queued. Rebuilds use snapshots plus a change-log boundary. The trade-off is fast relevance ranking versus stale permissions and index cost; never trust a tenant filter supplied only by the caller.

followups.q: Is filtering by tenant ID enough?
followups.a: No; document-level permissions and current authorization may also vary within a tenant.

followups.q: When is deletion complete?
followups.a: After authoritative state and every serving index or cache can no longer return the document.

questions.trap: Assuming asynchronous indexing makes access revocation safe without tracking deletion and ACL propagation lag.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.

questions.question: Design file synchronization across multiple devices with offline edits, version history and conflict resolution.
questions.answer: Clarify file size, edit granularity, offline duration, conflict policy and sharing permissions. Each client tracks a server version and uploads content-addressed chunks with a manifest; the service commits a new version only when the expected parent still matches. Concurrent edits branch rather than silently overwrite, and clients receive conflict metadata or merge only supported formats. Tombstones propagate deletions and prevent an old offline device from resurrecting removed files without an explicit restore action. Durable change cursors support reconnect and bounded delta sync. The trade-off is bandwidth-efficient chunking and offline availability versus metadata complexity and conflict UX. Access is checked on every manifest and chunk request.

followups.q: How do you handle two offline edits to the same file?
followups.a: Preserve both version branches or use a format-aware merge; never silently overwrite the newer version.

followups.q: Why propagate tombstones?
followups.a: They stop stale replicas from interpreting a missing file as a new upload and resurrecting it.

questions.trap: Using last-write-wins for arbitrary file content or syncing data without permission checks on chunk access.
questions.notes: Unverified HLD estimate; Design-round classification estimated.
